newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Life expectancy plunges in Russia, ex-Soviet world.
newsitem.headline: Life expectancy plunges in Russia, ex-Soviet world.

text.p: Life expectancy has plunged to its lowest in 15 years in Russia, the land of "smetana" heavy sour cream, deep-fried potatoes and heavy smokers, a survey by the United Nations health agency said.
The World Health Organisation in Geneva said life expectancy had dipped in all 15 republics of the former Soviet Union, but the worst hit was Russia.

The average Russian man could now expect to live 57.4 years compared to 61.1 years in 1981 -- and nearly 64 years before Mikhail Gorbachev stepped down and President Boris Yeltsin started Russia's painful transition to capitalism.
Health services were a cradle-to-grave right of every Soviet citizen, but they slipped into a crisis after the start of market reforms brought unemployment, disorder and stress.
New WHO data pointed to a growing health gap between East and West.
Men in western Europe could expect to live an average 73 years compared to 63 years for their East European counterparts.
Women in western Europe could look forward to live nearly 80 years compared to 74 years for women in eastern Europe.
WHO said sunny Australia and New Zealand had life expectancy of more than 80 years for women and more than 74 years for men.

Life expectancy was more than 75 years for men in Greece, Sweden and Switzerland and also in Israel, Japan and Australia, and more than 81 years for women in Canada, France, Japan, Spain and Switzerland.

The biggest killers of men were diseases of the circulatory system, mainly heart disorders and strokes, responsible for half of all male deaths -- highest in Russia, the Baltic republic of Latvia and Turkmenistan and lowest in Japan, France and Mexico.

Heart disease and strokes killed more women than men and were to blame for up to 70 percent of all female deaths -- peaking in former Soviet Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan in Central Asia and Russia and lowest in France, Japan and Canada.
WHO said the second biggest killer was cancer, the cause of between eight and 32 percent of all male deaths and between eight and 30 percent of all female deaths.

Britain, New Zealand and Hungary had the highest female mortality rates from cancer and Albania, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan the lowest. Cancer was the cause of a third of all male deaths in France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands.

WHO said respiratory diseases, mainly pneumonia, were the third biggest killer of men and women in the world, accounting for up to 15 percent of deaths. The worst hit were two mountainous Central Asian republics, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.
Traffic accidents were the cause of up to four percent of all deaths -- but in Russia more men died from committing suicide.
Suicide also took a heavy toll in Lithuania and Latvia, causing up to five percent of all male deaths.
Suicide rates were also high among women in Austria, Finland, Switzerland, Japan, Hungary, France, Sweden, Lithuania and Slovenia, causing two percent of deaths.
